title: Tcpdump

steps.q: You need to reduce a large capture to traffic involving one host. Which concept should you use first?
steps.why: Tcpdump uses Berkeley Packet Filter syntax to narrow packet data.

steps.q: What is the best reason to learn tcpdump syntax rather than memorize one command?
choices: Packet-analysis questions change, so you must build filters for the evidence you need
steps.why: The lab emphasizes using help and syntax to adapt packet capture and filtering to the investigative question.

steps.q: You have a pcap from a compromised web server. What can tcpdump help you inspect?
steps.why: Tcpdump can read saved captures and expose network and transport-layer information.

steps.q: What is the lab-level takeaway?
choices: Use packet filters to turn a large capture into targeted evidence
steps.why: The operational skill is isolating relevant traffic from a large packet set.

steps.q: Capture excerpt: 10.0.0.4.53000 > 198.51.100.2.443 Flags [S], then the same [S] three times. What should you investigate first?
choices: Why the SYN receives no observed reply
steps.why: Repeated SYNs suggest a missing response; filtering, routing, endpoint state, and capture position are possibilities.

steps.q: Your capture command used 'tcp port 443' but the browser used HTTP/3. Why might the transaction be absent?
choices: All browsers use ICMP for web traffic
The filter decrypts and discards TLS
HTTP/3 commonly uses UDP rather than TCP
steps.why: QUIC-based HTTP/3 uses UDP; a TCP-only capture excludes it.

title: Wireshark

steps.q: Which Wireshark capability helps reconstruct an application conversation?
steps.why: Following a stream reassembles the selected TCP conversation for analysis.

steps.q: Which filter is used after traffic is already captured?
steps.why: Wireshark display filters narrow what is shown from existing evidence.

steps.q: A capture includes an HTTP file transfer. Which capability may recover the transferred object?
steps.why: Wireshark can extract objects from supported protocols when the capture contains the necessary data.

steps.q: What is the central lesson of the lab?
choices: Use protocol dissection and statistics to move from traffic volume to meaningful conversations
GUI tools make protocol knowledge unnecessary
Every capture contains full decrypted TLS content
steps.why: Wireshark is powerful because it organizes and decodes packet evidence, but analysts still need protocol knowledge.

steps.q: Trace: client SYN, server SYN-ACK, client ACK, then client TLS ClientHello. Which event has not yet been demonstrated?
steps.why: The trace establishes transport and starts TLS, but shows no completed TLS or application authentication.

steps.q: A display filter hides packets in a saved capture. What happens when the filter is cleared?
choices: The router retransmits the entire capture
Previously hidden captured packets become visible again
steps.why: Display filters change the view rather than the captured evidence.

description: Independent guided workflow practice; not an official SANS lab or a live virtual machine.

title: AWS VPC Flow Logs

steps.q: What kind of evidence do VPC Flow Logs primarily provide?
steps.why: Flow logs summarize connections rather than providing packet payloads.

steps.q: Which question is flow data particularly good at answering?
choices: Which hosts made unusual numbers of outbound connections?
What exact command appeared inside an encrypted TLS session?
What password is stored in memory?
Which NTFS ACE denied a file?
steps.why: Flow data is excellent for large-scale communication patterns and outlier discovery.

steps.q: Why compare flow-log findings with packet captures?
choices: Each evidence type provides different levels of detail
Packet captures have no network metadata
Flow logs contain every payload byte
steps.why: Flows provide scale and summaries; pcaps provide packet-level detail.

steps.q: What mindset does the AI portion of the lab reinforce?
choices: Use AI as an analytical aid but verify conclusions against evidence
steps.why: The lab explicitly challenges AI-assisted analysis and emphasizes verification.

steps.q: Synthetic flow record: src=10.0.2.9 dst=198.51.100.8 dstport=443 protocol=6 action=REJECT. What does protocol 6 identify?
steps.why: The IP protocol number 6 identifies TCP. A port field and an IP protocol field are different namespaces.

steps.q: A flow record says ACCEPT for an outbound connection. What does this not establish?
choices: That the remote application completed the request
That the logged policy allowed the flow
steps.why: A network policy decision is not proof of application success or benign purpose.

title: Password Auditing

steps.q: What must commonly happen before an offline password audit can begin?
choices: Extract or convert the protected data into a hash format the cracking tool understands
steps.why: The lab uses conversion/extraction utilities before John or Hashcat can test guesses.

steps.q: Which two tools are central to the lab?
steps.why: The lab provides hands-on exposure to John and Hashcat.

steps.q: Why does account lockout not stop offline cracking of a copied hash?
choices: The attacker tests guesses locally without contacting the live authentication service
steps.why: Offline cracking bypasses online rate limiting and lockout mechanisms.

steps.q: What should you remember for GSEC?
choices: Hash extraction and password cracking are distinct steps
steps.why: A tool often must first extract/convert the stored verifier before candidate passwords can be tested.

steps.q: Two password verifiers use unique salts. Which attack cost is primarily increased across many accounts?
choices: Reusing precomputed results for identical passwords
Trying a single guess against one verifier
steps.why: Unique salts force per-salt computation. They do not remove the need for costly password hashing and strong passwords.

steps.q: An authorized password audit finds a recovered password. Which report detail is appropriate?
choices: The plaintext password in a public ticket
The password emailed to all employees
The password in every dashboard title
A controlled finding with remediation, without exposing the password broadly
steps.why: Treat recovered credentials as sensitive evidence, restrict access, and arrange resets and broader impact review.

title: Data Loss Prevention

steps.q: Which artifact can reveal who created or handled a document?
steps.why: Document metadata can expose creator and handling information.

steps.q: Which is an example of an overt marker?
steps.why: Overt markers are intentionally visible to the user.

steps.q: Why inspect hidden/contextual markers as well as visible labels?
choices: Sensitive files may contain provenance clues not obvious on the page
Hidden data cannot exist in documents
steps.why: DLP and investigations may rely on metadata, hidden content, and contextual clues.

steps.q: In Data Loss Prevention, which principle should guide your workflow?
choices: Data leakage analysis requires understanding content, context, metadata, and markings
DLP is only a firewall function
steps.why: DLP is broader than keyword blocking; context and provenance matter.

steps.q: Synthetic DLP event: action=blocked rule=customer-records destination=personal-storage. What should be checked next?
choices: Whether every network port should be opened
Whether all staff should be locked out
Whether the rule's name proves a breach
Whether the content and business context support the match
steps.why: Validate the classification, user context, destination, and action outcome before escalation or tuning.

steps.q: A DLP test uses a real customer database copied to a personal account. What is a safer test design?
choices: Disable logging to protect the tester
Publish the database as a checksum
Use approved synthetic data and controlled destinations
steps.why: Synthetic fixtures can exercise detection without creating the data exposure the control is intended to prevent.

title: Mobile Device Backup Recovery

steps.q: Why is an unencrypted mobile backup valuable to an investigator?
choices: It may expose messages, files, app data, and other artifacts without live-device interaction
steps.why: Backups can preserve a wide range of forensic artifacts.

steps.q: What changes if the backup is encrypted?
choices: You need the decryption credential and a tool capable of using it
The backup becomes a packet capture
steps.why: Encrypted backups require recovery of the password/key and compatible tooling.

steps.q: Why hash a recovered company document?
choices: To compare it reliably with known copies and establish integrity
steps.why: Cryptographic hashes can match artifacts and help demonstrate integrity.

steps.q: What is the practical lesson?
choices: Understand backup structure so you can triage data with appropriate tools
Only commercial forensic tools can examine backups
steps.why: The lab shows that understanding structure and artifacts matters as much as owning a specialized tool.

steps.q: A mobile backup extraction produces account tokens and messages. How should the output be handled?
choices: As an executable program that must be launched
As public training data by default
As sensitive evidence with restricted access and documented handling
As harmless because it came from a backup
steps.why: Backup data may contain credentials and personal content. Extraction does not reduce its sensitivity.

steps.q: A recovered record has a timestamp but no timezone documented. What should the timeline record?
choices: The original timestamp and the unresolved timezone assumption
A guessed timezone presented as certain
steps.why: Preserve original values and distinguish assumptions from verified conversions before correlating events.

title: Network Discovery

steps.q: Which tool is central to this lab?
steps.why: The lab builds experience with Nmap for discovery and mapping.

steps.q: Which capability helps identify unexpected services?
steps.why: Service mapping can reveal services that do not match expected port assignments or baselines.

steps.q: Why compare a current scan with an older scan?
choices: To detect configuration or exposure changes
steps.why: Differences between scans can identify newly exposed services or other drift.

steps.q: What is the high-value security lesson?
choices: Discovery data is useful for both attackers and defenders, so defenders should know their own exposure first
steps.why: The same discovery techniques attackers use can help defenders maintain accurate exposure awareness.

steps.q: An authorized scan reports 443/tcp open and 445/tcp filtered. What does filtered mean here?
choices: Probes did not establish a definitive open or closed state because of filtering or similar interference
No host exists at that address
steps.why: Filtered is not equivalent to closed. Network controls or absent responses limit the inference.

steps.q: A service banner claims an old version, but the administrator says a fix was backported. What should you do?
choices: Assume the banner always proves exploitability
Validate patch status and the actual vulnerable behavior using approved methods
steps.why: Vendors may backport fixes without changing upstream-looking banners. Validate the condition and retain evidence.

title: Binary File Analysis and Characterization

steps.q: Which two tools are intentionally sufficient for the initial lab characterization?
steps.why: The lab uses basic available tools to collect evidence before deeper malware analysis.

steps.q: What can strings from an executable reveal?
choices: URLs, domains, paths, commands, and other clues
steps.why: Strings can expose useful indicators but require interpretation.

steps.q: How should AI be used in this lab?
choices: As a reasoning aid to propose investigative steps, with evidence used to validate them
steps.why: The lab deliberately separates AI guidance from analyst evidence.

steps.q: What is the central workflow lesson?
choices: Gather observable evidence before forming strong conclusions
Run the executable immediately on production
Assume calculator-like behavior means the file is safe
steps.why: Initial characterization should be evidence-driven and cautious.

steps.q: Static strings include a URL. What is the strongest conclusion supported by that artifact alone?
choices: The binary definitely connected to the URL
The URL text exists in the binary
The URL is the attacker controller
steps.why: Static content does not prove execution. Correlate with code paths and controlled behavioral analysis.

steps.q: A suspicious binary has the same SHA-256 as a preserved evidence copy. What does that support?
choices: Proof that it ran on the victim
A guarantee that the file is benign
Byte-level integrity between the compared copies
The identity of the original author
steps.why: Matching hashes support sameness of content under the hash's security assumptions, not intent or execution.

title: Web App Exploitation

steps.q: What vulnerability is the focus of the lab?
steps.why: The lab demonstrates a simple SQL injection flaw.

steps.q: What architectural tiers are present in the lab application?
choices: Nginx web tier, PHP application logic, and MySQL database
steps.why: The lab uses a three-tier web application design.

steps.q: What design mistake enables the attack?
choices: Unsafe input reaches a database query without adequate separation/validation
steps.why: Untrusted input must not be allowed to alter query syntax.

steps.q: What should you remember for defense?
choices: Use parameterized queries and enforce security on the server
Block apostrophes as the only defense
steps.why: Prepared/parameterized statements are the core structural defense against SQL injection.

steps.q: Synthetic request: GET /invoice/208 returns another customer's invoice to user A. What should the lab fix validate?
choices: Authorization for user A on invoice 208
Only that the button is hidden
steps.why: Object access must be checked server-side for every request, regardless of identifier syntax.

steps.q: After parameterizing a database query, which test best validates the change?
choices: Trust a code comment saying secure
Verify hostile input stays data and legitimate requests still work
Check only that the login page looks identical
steps.why: A regression test should exercise the original injection condition and expected normal behavior.

title: SIEM Log Analysis

steps.q: Why centralize logs?
choices: To correlate activity across systems and make large datasets searchable
To eliminate the need for endpoint logs
steps.why: Centralized logging creates a broader investigative view.

steps.q: Which stack does the lab use?
choices: Elastic Stack with Elasticsearch and Kibana
steps.why: The lab uses Elastic components to search and analyze security events.

steps.q: What is an investigative lead?
choices: An anomaly or pattern that merits further examination
steps.why: SIEM analysis generates leads that must be validated against additional evidence.

steps.q: What limits even an excellent SIEM?
steps.why: A SIEM cannot analyze evidence that was never collected.

steps.q: Synthetic log: 08:00 user=pat fail; 08:01 user=pat fail; 08:02 user=pat success; all src=203.0.113.7. What is the next useful correlation?
choices: Pat's device context and activity after the success
steps.why: The sequence is suspicious but not conclusive. Context and subsequent actions help distinguish compromise from user error.

steps.q: A parser accidentally maps destination_ip into source_ip. What happens to source-based detections?
choices: They may attribute or correlate activity incorrectly
steps.why: Field extraction errors undermine rules and investigations. Validate normalization against original events.

title: Hashing and Cryptographic Validation

steps.q: What does a file hash primarily help demonstrate?
steps.why: A cryptographic hash can detect changes to file contents.

steps.q: Which tool is used in the lab for signing/verification operations?
steps.why: GPG supports key generation and digital signature operations.

steps.q: Which key does the signer use to create a normal digital signature?
steps.why: The private key creates the signature; the public key verifies it.

steps.q: What combination does signature verification support?
steps.why: A valid signature provides evidence that the signed content was not altered and corresponds to the signing key.

steps.q: Expected SHA-256 is A; acquired copy hashes to B. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Change B to A in the report
Stop relying on integrity and investigate acquisition or reference differences
steps.why: A mismatch requires explanation: the data, acquisition, or trusted reference may differ. Preserve evidence and document findings.

steps.q: A detached signature verifies, but the key fingerprint is unknown. What remains necessary?
choices: Assume any valid key belongs to the publisher
Authenticate the signing key's identity through a trusted channel
steps.why: Signature mathematics and identity trust are separate. Verify the expected fingerprint or trusted certification path.

title: Encryption and Decryption

steps.q: What security property is the lab primarily applying to stored data?
steps.why: Encryption at rest protects stored information from unauthorized reading.

steps.q: What is the key distinction between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
choices: Symmetric uses a shared secret; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
steps.why: The two models differ primarily in key structure and operational use.

steps.q: When encrypting to a recipient using public-key cryptography, which key is normally used for confidentiality?
steps.why: Data encrypted for a recipient is protected using their public key so only the matching private key can decrypt it.

steps.q: What should you remember?
choices: Encryption is reversible with the proper key; hashing is generally one-way
steps.why: GSEC questions often test the property each cryptographic mechanism actually provides.

steps.q: A sender encrypts a message using a recipient's public key. Which secret is normally needed to decrypt it?
steps.why: Public-key encryption targets a key pair. Protect the recipient private key and verify the intended public key binding.

steps.q: Decryption fails after a ciphertext byte is changed in an authenticated encryption scheme. What is the likely intended behavior?
choices: Reject tampered ciphertext rather than release unauthenticated plaintext
Recover the key from the changed byte
steps.why: Authentication failure should prevent use of modified data. Do not bypass the integrity check to force decryption.

title: Intrusion Detection and Network Security Monitoring

steps.q: Which tool is most strongly associated with signature/rule matching?
steps.why: Snort uses rules to match known traffic patterns.

steps.q: Which tool is most strongly associated with rich protocol logs and behavior-oriented hunting?
steps.why: Zeek generates structured protocol telemetry useful for correlation and hunting.

steps.q: Why does the lab expose you to both tools?
choices: They perform exactly the same function
steps.why: Signature alerts and protocol telemetry answer different security questions.

steps.q: What is the high-level lesson?
choices: Prevention is ideal, but timely detection is mandatory for effective response
Detection removes the need for response
Logs are useful only for troubleshooting

steps.q: A sensor records one signature match on a test exploit request. What additional check evaluates prevention?
choices: Whether the protected application received or processed the request
Whether the analyst recognizes the source IP
Whether the alert color is red
Whether the rule name contains block

steps.q: A network sensor is connected to the wrong mirror port and sees no server traffic. What does a quiet dashboard indicate?
choices: A possible visibility gap, not evidence of no attacks
That all traffic is encrypted with perfect security
steps.why: Validate sensor placement, packet counts, and expected test traffic before trusting detection silence.

title: Windows Process Exploration

steps.q: Which tool does the lab use to inspect Windows processes?
steps.why: System Informer provides detailed Windows process visibility.

steps.q: Which process relationship is a strong investigative lead?
choices: Office application spawning PowerShell with an encoded command
Signed system binary in its normal path
steps.why: Unexpected parent-child relationships can indicate malicious execution chains.

steps.q: Why inspect process memory or associated connections?
choices: They can reveal network destinations, strings, or files tied to suspicious behavior
steps.why: Process context can connect execution activity to network or file artifacts.

steps.q: In Windows Process Exploration, which principle should guide your workflow?
choices: Know normal process behavior so abnormal execution stands out
steps.why: Baseline awareness and context are essential to process triage.

steps.q: Process tree: winword.exe -> powershell.exe -> unknown.exe. What does this justify?
choices: Investigation of document-triggered execution and related evidence
An automatic conclusion that every Office document is malicious
A claim that the user was offline
Immediate deletion of all Windows binaries
steps.why: Unexpected parent-child relationships are useful leads. Inspect command lines, signer, file path, network activity, and user context.

steps.q: A process is named svchost.exe but runs from a user's Downloads folder. What is the relevant next check?
choices: Validate path, signature, parentage, and behavior
Trust the name because it looks familiar
steps.why: Names can be impersonated. Provenance and execution context matter more than a familiar filename alone.

title: Windows Filesystem Permissions

steps.q: Which two permission layers can both affect remote SMB access?
steps.why: Remote file access can be constrained by both share-level and NTFS ACLs.

steps.q: What is a DACL made of?
steps.why: A DACL contains ACEs that allow or deny access.

steps.q: What is a common security failure with permissions?
choices: Troubleshooting causes overly broad access that is never corrected
steps.why: Temporary permission changes often become permanent exposure if not reviewed.

steps.q: What does the lab teach?
choices: Identify and remediate unsafe filesystem ACLs rather than merely observe them
steps.why: The lab focuses on detecting and fixing incorrect access-control configuration.

steps.q: Share permission Read; NTFS permission Full Control; no other rules. Can the user modify the file through that share?
choices: No, the share restricts remote access to Read
Yes, NTFS always overrides share permissions
No, because shares never support writes
steps.why: Both layers apply to remote access; the share restriction limits this simplified example.

steps.q: A new deny entry blocks a business group unexpectedly. What should be reviewed before adding broader allow entries?
choices: Explicit denies, inheritance, and group membership
steps.why: Additional allows may not resolve deny behavior. Analyze the actual access-check inputs and scope of the deny.

title: Applying Windows System Security Policies

steps.q: Why are known-good security baselines valuable?
choices: Unauthorized configuration drift becomes easier to detect
They remove the need for logging
steps.why: Configuration management creates an expected state for comparison.

steps.q: What should happen after applying a desired security configuration?
choices: Validate that the system actually matches the desired state
steps.why: Verification is required to prove the intended settings took effect.

steps.q: How does change control support security investigations?
steps.why: A well-maintained change record helps distinguish authorized drift from potentially malicious changes.

steps.q: What is the core lesson?
choices: Consistent configuration plus validation improves both prevention and detection
Configuration management is only administrative paperwork
steps.why: Secure configuration management creates enforceable and observable system state.

steps.q: A security GPO exists but a host does not apply it. What should the lab check?

Only that a password was changed
Link scope, security filtering, and resultant policy
Only that the GPO has a descriptive name
steps.why: Policy existence does not prove application. Scope, filtering, processing, and replication can affect results.

steps.q: A baseline disables a required legacy service. What is the best resolution?
choices: Assess the dependency and approve a narrow documented exception or replacement
steps.why: A scoped exception or replacement can manage business needs without abandoning unrelated protections.

title: Linux Permissions

steps.q: What numeric value represents read permission?
steps.why: Linux numeric permissions use read=4, write=2, execute=1.

steps.q: What does chmod change?
steps.why: chmod changes the permission mode of files or directories.

steps.q: Why do set-UID, set-GID, and sticky permissions deserve special attention?
choices: They modify normal execution or directory permission behavior
steps.why: Special permission bits can change privilege or deletion behavior and therefore affect security.

steps.q: What is the central lesson?
choices: Understand owner, group, others, and special bits rather than memorizing isolated chmod examples
steps.why: Linux access control depends on interpreting the complete permission and ownership context.

steps.q: Mode shown: drwxrwxrwt on a shared directory. What does the trailing t represent?
steps.why: The sticky bit restricts who may remove entries in a shared writable directory.

steps.q: A regular file is -rw-r-----. What is its octal mode before considering special bits or ACLs?
steps.why: Owner rw is 6, group r is 4, others none is 0.

title: Linux Containers

steps.q: Why can container-local logs be fragile evidence?
choices: Containers are ephemeral and may be destroyed or recreated
steps.why: Evidence stored only inside a short-lived container may disappear with it.

steps.q: What is a central security distinction between a container and a VM?
choices: Containers share the host kernel; VMs generally run separate guest kernels
steps.why: Shared-kernel architecture changes the isolation boundary.

steps.q: What is the better logging design for important container workloads?
choices: Persist or forward logs outside the ephemeral container
Store logs only in /tmp inside the container
steps.why: Externalization preserves logs across container lifecycle events.

steps.q: In Linux Containers, which principle should guide your workflow?
choices: Container lifecycle design directly affects evidence retention and incident response
steps.why: Security architecture must account for container ephemerality and host dependencies.

steps.q: Container config shows Privileged=true and a read/write host-root mount. What should be prioritized?

steps.why: Privileged mode and broad host mounts undermine isolation and can expose the host to container compromise.

steps.q: An image tag changed overnight without an application change request. What control improves reproducibility?
choices: Pin and verify the intended image digest through the release process
steps.why: Tags can move. Verified digest selection ties deployment to specific content and requires deliberate updates.

title: Linux Logging and Auditing

steps.q: How does audit logging differ from many traditional system logs?
